solution:
A circle with centre at the origin and radius \(r\) has equation \(x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\).
Here \(r=4\), so \(r^{2}=16\).
\(\therefore\) the equation of the circle is \(x^{2}+y^{2}=16\).

The radius is the distance between the centre \((-3,\ -3)\) and the point \((-3,\ -6)\) on the circle:
\(r=\sqrt{(-3+3)^{2}+(-6+3)^{2}}=\sqrt{0+9}=3\).
Hence \((x+3)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=9\)
\(x^{2}+6x+9+y^{2}+6y+9=9\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}+6x+6y+9=0\).

Compare \(x^{2}+y^{2}=25\) with \(x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\), the circle with centre at the origin.
So \(r^{2}=25\), giving \(r=5\).
\(\therefore\) centre \(=(0,\ 0)\) and radius \(=5\).

Compare \(\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(y+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{1}{36}\) with \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\).
Then \(h=\dfrac{1}{2},\ k=-\dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(r^{2}=\dfrac{1}{36}\), so \(r=\dfrac{1}{6}\).
\(\therefore\) centre \(=\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\ -\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\) and radius \(=\dfrac{1}{6}\).

If a circle touches the Y-axis (the line \(x=0\)), its radius equals the perpendicular distance of the centre from that axis.
For centre \((a,\ b)\) this distance is \(|a|\), so \(r=|a|\) and \(r^{2}=a^{2}\).
Hence \((x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=a^{2}\)
\(x^{2}-2ax+a^{2}+y^{2}-2by+b^{2}=a^{2}\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}-2ax-2by+b^{2}=0\).

A circle touching the X-axis has radius equal to the distance of its centre from that axis, i.e. \(|k|\).
For centre \((-2,\ 3)\), \(r=|3|=3\).
Hence \((x+2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=9\)
\(x^{2}+4x+4+y^{2}-6y+9=9\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}+4x-6y+4=0\).

Let the centre be \((h,\ 0)\), since it lies on the X-axis.
The circle passes through the origin, so \(r=\sqrt{(h-0)^{2}+0^{2}}=|h|\).
Given \(r=4\), we get \(|h|=4\), so \(h=4\) or \(h=-4\) — there are two such circles.
For \(h=4\): \((x-4)^{2}+y^{2}=16\), i.e. \(x^{2}+y^{2}-8x=0\).
For \(h=-4\): \((x+4)^{2}+y^{2}=16\), i.e. \(x^{2}+y^{2}+8x=0\).
\(\therefore\) the required equation is \(x^{2}+y^{2}\pm 8x=0\).

If a circle touches a line, its radius is the perpendicular distance from the centre to that line.
\(r=\dfrac{|8(3)-15(1)+25|}{\sqrt{8^{2}+(-15)^{2}}}=\dfrac{|24-15+25|}{\sqrt{289}}=\dfrac{34}{17}=2\).
Hence \((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=4\)
\(x^{2}-6x+9+y^{2}-2y+1=4\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-2y+6=0\).

Every diameter passes through the centre, so the centre is the point of intersection of the two given diameters.
Solve \(2x+y=6\) and \(3x+2y=4\): from the first, \(y=6-2x\); substituting,
\(3x+2(6-2x)=4\ \Rightarrow\ -x+12=4\ \Rightarrow\ x=8\), and then \(y=6-16=-10\).
So the centre is \((8,\ -10)\) and \(r=9\).
\((x-8)^{2}+(y+10)^{2}=81\)
\(x^{2}-16x+64+y^{2}+20y+100=81\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}-16x+20y+83=0\).

First find the end points of the chord, i.e. where \(y=2x\) meets \(x^{2}+y^{2}-10x=0\).
Substituting \(y=2x\): \(x^{2}+4x^{2}-10x=0\ \Rightarrow\ 5x(x-2)=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=0\) or \(x=2\).
So the end points are \(A(0,\ 0)\) and \(B(2,\ 4)\).
With \(AB\) as diameter, the equation is \((x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})+(y-y_{1})(y-y_{2})=0\):
\((x-0)(x-2)+(y-0)(y-4)=0\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y=0\).

If a circle of radius 4 touches both axes, the centre is at distance 4 from each axis, so it is \((\pm 4,\ \pm 4)\).
The centre lies in the third quadrant, where both coordinates are negative, so the centre is \((-4,\ -4)\).
\((x+4)^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=16\)
\(x^{2}+8x+16+y^{2}+8y+16=16\)
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}+8x+8y+16=0\).

[Textbook misprint: the question carries a stray sub-item label (a) mid-sentence, between circle and passing through, with no matching (b) anywhere in the exercise — Q7 is a single undivided question. Preserved as printed; the sentence reads straight through without it.]

Let the circle be \(x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0\).
It passes through the origin, so \(c=0\).
Put \(y=0\) to find where it meets the X-axis: \(x^{2}+2gx=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=0\) or \(x=-2g\), so the x-intercept is \(-2g\).
Given \(-2g=4\), so \(g=-2\).
Put \(x=0\): \(y^{2}+2fy=0\ \Rightarrow\ y=0\) or \(y=-2f\), so the y-intercept is \(-2f\).
Given \(-2f=-5\), so \(f=\dfrac{5}{2}\).
\(\therefore\ x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+5y=0\).

The coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) must be made 1, so divide throughout by 4:
\(x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-2y-6=0\).
Comparing with \(x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0\): \(g=-3,\ f=-1,\ c=-6\).
Centre \(=(-g,\ -f)=(3,\ 1)\).
Radius \(=\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c}=\sqrt{9+1+6}=\sqrt{16}=4\).
\(\therefore\) centre \(=(3,\ 1)\) and radius \(=4\).

In the given equation the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are equal (both 3) and there is no \(xy\) term, so it can be a circle. Divide throughout by 3:
\(x^{2}+y^{2}+4x+6y-\dfrac{11}{3}=0\).
Comparing with \(x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0\): \(g=2,\ f=3,\ c=-\dfrac{11}{3}\).
Now \(g^{2}+f^{2}-c=4+9+\dfrac{11}{3}=\dfrac{50}{3}>0\), so the radius is real and positive.
Hence the equation represents a circle, with centre \((-2,\ -3)\) and radius \(\sqrt{\dfrac{50}{3}}=\dfrac{5\sqrt{6}}{3}\).

Find the circle through the first three points and then test the fourth.
Let it be \(x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0\).
For \((1,\ 0)\): \(1+2g+c=0\) ... (1)
For \((3,\ -2)\): \(13+6g-4f+c=0\) ... (2)
For \((-1,\ -2)\): \(5-2g-4f+c=0\) ... (3)
(2) \(-\) (3): \(8+8g=0\ \Rightarrow\ g=-1\); then (1) gives \(c=1\), and (3) gives \(5+2-4f+1=0\ \Rightarrow\ f=2\).
So the circle through the three points is \(x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+4y+1=0\).
Now test \((1,\ -4)\): \(1+16-2-16+1=0\), which is satisfied.
Since all four points lie on this one circle, they are concyclic (the circle has centre \((1,\ -2)\) and radius 2).

\(x^{2}+y^{2}=9\) has centre \((0,\ 0)\) and radius \(r=3\).
For a circle \(x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\) the parametric equations are \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\).
\(\therefore\ x=3\cos\theta,\ y=3\sin\theta\), where \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

Here \(g=1,\ f=-2,\ c=-4\), so the centre is \((-1,\ 2)\) and the radius is \(\sqrt{1+4+4}=3\).
For a circle with centre \((h,\ k)\) and radius \(r\), the parametric equations are \(x=h+r\cos\theta,\ y=k+r\sin\theta\).
\(\therefore\ x=-1+3\cos\theta,\ y=2+3\sin\theta\), where \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

\((x-3)^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=25\) has centre \((3,\ -4)\) and radius \(r=5\).
Using \(x=h+r\cos\theta,\ y=k+r\sin\theta\):
\(\therefore\ x=3+5\cos\theta,\ y=-4+5\sin\theta\), where \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

Divide throughout by 3 to make the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) equal to 1:
\(x^{2}+y^{2}-\dfrac{4}{3}x+2y-\dfrac{4}{3}=0\).
So \(g=-\dfrac{2}{3},\ f=1,\ c=-\dfrac{4}{3}\), giving centre \(\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\ -1\right)\) and
\(r=\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{9}+1+\dfrac{4}{3}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{25}{9}}=\dfrac{5}{3}\).
Using \(x=h+r\cos\theta,\ y=k+r\sin\theta\):
\(\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{5}{3}\cos\theta,\ y=-1+\dfrac{5}{3}\sin\theta\), where \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

For \(x^{2}+y^{2}-3x+2y=0\) we have \(g=-\dfrac{3}{2},\ f=1,\ c=0\).
Since \(c=0\), the origin lies on the circle, so a tangent there exists.
The tangent at \((x_{1},\ y_{1})\) is \(xx_{1}+yy_{1}+g(x+x_{1})+f(y+y_{1})+c=0\).
At \((0,\ 0)\): \(0+0-\dfrac{3}{2}(x+0)+1(y+0)+0=0\)
\(-\dfrac{3}{2}x+y=0\)
Multiplying by \(-2\): \(\therefore\ 3x-2y=0\).

Step 1: \((1,\ 2)\) lies on the circle, since \(1+4+5(1)-7(2)+4=1+4+5-14+4=0\).
It also lies on the line, since \(7(1)-3(2)-1=0\).
Step 2: For the circle, \(g=\dfrac{5}{2},\ f=-\dfrac{7}{2},\ c=4\). The tangent at \((x_{1},\ y_{1})\) is \(xx_{1}+yy_{1}+g(x+x_{1})+f(y+y_{1})+c=0\), so at \((1,\ 2)\):
\(x+2y+\dfrac{5}{2}(x+1)-\dfrac{7}{2}(y+2)+4=0\)
\(\left(1+\dfrac{5}{2}\right)x+\left(2-\dfrac{7}{2}\right)y+\left(\dfrac{5}{2}-7+4\right)=0\)
\(\dfrac{7}{2}x-\dfrac{3}{2}y-\dfrac{1}{2}=0\)
Multiplying by 2: \(7x-3y-1=0\).
This is exactly the given line. Hence the line \(7x-3y-1=0\) touches the circle at \((1,\ 2)\).
